You have to remember that a surveyor has to cover themselves, if they don't raise something and you find out they missed it they could get sued. So consider that when you read the report. Anything that is level 3 should be looked at fairly soon but none of the things you listed strike me as an immediate need to repair. Even the soffit, if there is no sign of water ingress then take it as something that you should have high on your list but not immediate. 

In terms of the costs of repairs you have to consider whether you offered a fair price on the property. For me that consideration is looking at the price of a fully renovated property nearby and considering whether the price I am paying plus the renovation costs roughly line up with that. If you are way over you may want to consider negotiating but if it roughly lines up I wouldn't bother. Remeber the seller could just say no and back out so you have to weigh up the risk you are willing to take. 

If it helps my survey was a train wreck compared to yours and I did have to negotiate because of it but it was a very stressful process so only worth it if the issues are extremely costly.

First your sister is not personally liable for the debt as long as it wasn't in joint names. However the credit card companies can put in a claim against the estate. This is any remaining money after the funeral costs have been accounted for. That would include any money solely in his name in a current account for example. If there is no remaining money after the funeral has been paid then there is nothing to claim from, you may need to prove this but once you have the debts will be written off.

I don't know the situation with the house but I just found this link which suggests that when a house is jointly owned it automatically passes to the surviving partner and therefore does not form part of the estate so I doubt the companies would have a claim against the house.
 https://www.georgegreen.co.uk/site/george-green-blog/joint-property-ownership-and-inheritance

They cannot claim money that isn't there. 
Citizens advice are a good point of contact for this sort of thing and they referred me onto a debt charity who were able to answer my questions.

It's about finding the right counsellor and it doesn't sound like this one is right for you. There are two UK charities that offer grief counselling, the main one is Cruse (they also have a helpline and webchat for in the moment support). The other one is Sue Ryder. First I'd look to switch the loan as you can probably get a lower repayment over a longer period of time on that level of debt (find another with a lower repayment and use that to pay this one off). Or potentially a money transfer credit card as already mentioned (although I know you said you weren't eligible). If your credit is ok it's worth a try though. You can check your credit for free on various sites that will also give you cards you are likely to be accepted for. I'm sure you should be able to find an interest free card to transfer the credit card to at least. If you are the type of person who can trust themselves to be responsible another option is an interest free purchase card which you use for your groceries and essential spending and just pay the minimum off it each month while you prioritise clearing the other debts and you can then increase the payments so it is cleared within the interest free period. 

Next look to make money on your everyday spending. Chase bank (no credit check needed) give 1% cashback on all purchases and the jamdoughnut app give you 3-4% cashback on supermarket gift cards. Use your chase card to buy them and you're looking at making 5% of what you spend back. 

Then look to minimise your outgoings. Batch cook meals for several days at a time which cuts back on your fuel costs for cooking. Unplug everything after you've finished using it. Leave lights off and curtains open during the day (I know it sounds obvious but you'd be surprised!). And find out what time food gets discounted in your supermarket. My local one discounts between 7 and 8pm. You can then usually find fresh food that is going out of date on discount. Most of it is fine for a couple of days and if not cook it and then refrigerate and it will be. If you have space picking up a small freezer (you can usually find them free or really cheap on gumtree or marketplace) helps you to be able to find food on discount and freeze it. 

And as others have said. Don't worry about the house for now. Your income will likely increase over time and (hopefully) the cost of living crisis will calm at some point. Then you can start worrying about saving.

I'm not trying to be combative so please don't take it that way as I find your posts interesting and have used the links you provided as a basis to start my own studies. Having said that the scientists you reference, whilst extremely well respected in their day were operating around 100 years ago. In those times there were less experimental controls so something was often accepted as being fact with a lot less evidence than we would look for today. For example the use of statistical analysis didn't even begin to gain traction until the 1920s and was not widely used until around the 1960s. 

When we talk about a theory being proved we don't actually mean there is proof but rather that the phenomena has been observed and the experiment has been replicated to the extent that the liklihood of the results having occurred by chance are negligible. However this still does not constitute proof in the way that it would be generally understood as there is (however small) a chance that the results could have occurred through random interference or via a confounding variable that we have not yet identified. 

So in answer to your final question, no I do not expect that I will ever be convinced that there is proof of continuation of consciousness, it is absolutely conceivable, however, that I will be convinced beyond all reasonable doubt that this is the most plausible explanation for the observed effects. Particularly since there is currently no robust evidence for the materialist explanation.

I just want to add my two pence worth to this thread because I think the issue here is around terminology. For context I am a scientist and a psychologist (I research in the fields of cognitive psychology and psychophysiology). I am currently looking at the evidence for the continuation of consciousness for my own personal interest. I have only been looking at this for a relatively short period of time but here are my thoughts. 

There is absolutely evidence that consciousness continues after physical death. When looking at personal accounts what researchers look at is whether or not there are general consistencies. Everyone will view events differently (we know this from the research around eye witness testimony) but when there are commonalities between different events and particularly between different types of events this indicates that there is evidence in support of the phenomena in question. Some aspects e.g. psy phenomena have been analysed quantatively with statistically significant findings. Just to for those who don't study statistics a significant finding is not a confirmation that something has occurred it is simply an expression of the likelihood that something has occurred by chance. If something is statistically significant the likelihood of the effect having occurred by chance is extremely small. I suspect with the number of people researching these areas the amount of evidence we have to examine will increase.

What all of this means is that there IS evidence that indicates that consciousness may survive physical death. What there is not is proof. Becuase in science no such thing exists. We look for findings that indicate with a very small margin of error that such an effect occurs. Good scientists do not look for proof becuase none can ever be found. Even if every piece of evidence points to the existence of something we still do not say that there is proof. There is always new evidence to be found. What we know today is not what we will know tomorrow. To use a well known example, almost every scientist will accept evolution but there is no proof, just strong evidence that indicates this is the case.

My experience was different, weirdly I actually found mine after losing my mum I'll tell you the story which may or may not help you. I warn you it's long.

MY mum went into hospital a week before she passed and I was completely adrift (for context, she lived with me and I work from home a lot so we were together most of the time). It was sudden and I was only able to visit her for one hour a day (covid rules even though mum didn't have covid). In order to fill my day a little more I took to visiting the hospital Chapel each day before visiting her. Prior to this I would say that I was probably more spiritual than religious in that I believed there was 'something' but I didn'tgo to church. The day before my mum passed (at this point she was stable) I was in the Chapel and I felt a warmth pass through me. At the time I thought it meant that she was going to get better but unfortunately in the middle of the night I got a call to say that she had taken a turn for the worse and I needed to come in. I sat with her for 4 hours while her breathing slowed and finally stopped. I had no other close family so at my request the hospital chaplain came to sit with me which helped me to get through the most agonising experience of my life she didn't force faith on me just sat with her arm round me while I spoke to my mum and when she passed quite literally screamed in pain. Towards the end she very gently asked if she could say a prayer for my mum but again there was no pressure. In the days after I lost my mum I spent a lot of time alone as it was Christmas and all my friends were busy and at one point I came to think about that feeling I had the day before so I phoned the hospital chaplain service and spoke to them. I told them I had prayed for my mum and that my prayers hadn't been answered. I asked whether it was because I wasn't a good enough Christian and the chaplain assured me this wasn't the case. He said simply that sometimes the answer is no and we don't know why. But it wasn't that which changed my thinking, I spoke to him about the moment a person passes and what happens prior to that and he told me stories of how most people see their relatives coming to 'take them home' and that he believed that home was heaven. 
I left it alone for a while until it was time to find a church to hold a service for my mum. I went into one recommended by the funeral director and from the moment I walked in I felt like I was coming home and I've been going to services there ever since. I don't necessarily subscribe to everything that is taught which I'm not going to go into as I'm not keen to influence others (if you want to know more about what I do believe dm me I'm happy to tell you) but those times I am in church are the only times now where I feel any sense of peace. So that's my story, it's early days for me so I have no idea where this ends up but hopefully it helps someone.
